items.title: Concept: a stage computed from facts
items.body:
Instead of a status column that commands overwrite, this app stores **facts** (intake completed, each verification's result, the decision, each condition, disbursement and hand-off times) and derives the stage from them. That keeps the stage consistent with the data, but it moves all of the policy into one function, and in that function the **order of the rules is the policy**.

Open `reconcileWorkflow` and write its rules down as a numbered list: the condition each one tests and the stage it returns. Then make yourself a few snapshots on paper (a funded loan with a late decision, an approved file with a problem condition, an approved file whose check result changes) and walk each through your list.

Next read `reconcileAndPersistStage` in the command service. Note exactly which comparison decides whether a row update and an `ApplicationTransition` are written. Finally, for `recordDecision` and `disburseApplication`, note which checks run before the transaction opens and what each refuses.

excerpts.quote: Stage is a function of facts.

readMore.why: The pure reconciler: read every rule in order.

items.title: Why the route refuses a loan officer before the service is asked
items.body:
The submit route declares `permission: "application:submit"`. `createRouteHandler` asserts that permission before calling the handler, and in the role table only BORROWER has it. A LOAN_OFFICER therefore gets **403** from the wrapper. The service's own check, which would let borrowers and loan officers through, never runs. The concepts doc notes that this inner check contradicts the matrix.

- *200* would be true only if the wrapper did not check permissions.
- *403 from the service* is wrong: the service is never reached, and it does not check the creator.
- *400 for confirmReady* is wrong: the body schema requires `true`, and the request fails before it is parsed.

items.title: Why a huge requested amount is a 500
items.body:
The create schema only requires `requestedAmount` to be positive. One trillion passes validation and reaches the insert, where the `Decimal(12,2)` column (at most ten digits before the point) overflows and PostgreSQL rejects the value. Prisma raises an error that is neither a `ZodError` nor an `AppError`, so `errorResponse` logs it and returns **500** "Internal server error."

- *400 out of range* would need a `.max()` on the schema.
- *Capped* and *stored as a float* are wrong: the database refuses the value instead of changing it.

items.title: How one borrower can give another access
items.body:
For borrowers, visibility is "some party on this application has my user id". The create schema lets each party carry an optional `userId`, and nothing checks that it belongs to the caller. Borrower A can therefore set the co-applicant's `userId` to B's id, and B now sees the application. User ids are easy to find, because `GET /api/session` lists the demo users.

- *Only the creator can read* is wrong: the rule is party membership, not authorship.
- *After a loan officer approves the link* is wrong: there is no such step.
- *Checked against the caller* is wrong: the schema accepts any non-empty string.

items.title: Concept: who may call what, and what they can see
items.body:
Three separate mechanisms decide what a request can do.

**The route wrapper.** `createRouteHandler` in `src/lib/http/route-handler.ts` resolves the session, applies the permission the route declares, runs the handler and maps errors to statuses. List the permission each route under `src/app/api/` declares, then compare it with the role table in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`. Look for role checks written inside the service too, and ask which one runs first.

**Record visibility.** `buildApplicationVisibilityWhere` in the repository restricts what some roles can read. Note the rule for each role, and where a party's `userId` comes from when an application is created.

**Provider events.** `ingestExternalVerificationEvent` takes simulated provider results. Find the two comparisons on `providerSequence` and note which operator each uses, what is stored in each case, and which actor id is passed on to the transition.

Finally note which kinds of error become 400, which keep their own status, and which become 500.

excerpts.quote: Each route declares one permission in its options object.

readMore.why: Session, permission and error handling for every route.
The visibility predicate and query shapes.

items.title: Why a late failed check pulls an approved file back
items.body:
The newer event is applied, so EMPLOYMENT_CHECK is now FAILED. On reconcile, the verification rule sits above every decision rule: it fires when any verification has FAILED, or a required type is missing or not PASSED. It returns VERIFICATION with a reason naming the failed type, whatever the recorded decision says.

- *APPROVED stays* is wrong: the decision is a fact, but the stage is derived, and the verification rule wins.
- *CONDITIONS* is for failed or open closing conditions, not verifications.
- *DENIED* needs a DECLINED decision or `deniedAt`; a failed check alone does not decline.

items.title: Who a provider-driven transition is credited to
items.body:
After storing the event, the command calls `reconcileAndPersistStage` with an actor id of `null` when the event was applied, and the user's id when it was not. `createTransition` sets `triggeredBySystem` to `actorUserId === null`. An applied event that changes the stage therefore produces a transition with no user and `triggeredBySystem: true`. The audit log row for the same event still names the loan officer.

- *The loan officer* is who the stale-event path and the audit log record, not the applied transition.
- *The provider reference* is stored on the verification, not used as an actor.
- *No transition* is wrong: a stage change always writes one.

items.title: Why a funded loan can still end up DENIED
items.body:
`recordDecision` refuses only when the derived stage is VERIFICATION, which a funded loan is not, so the decline is saved. The reconciler's first rule checks for a DECLINED decision or `deniedAt` before the rules for hand-off and disbursement. The application therefore becomes DENIED even though `disbursedAt` is set. The guided reading path calls this out: moving the DENIED rule below the funding rules would change the policy.

- *DISBURSEMENT* would need the funding rule first.
- *400* is wrong: nothing in the decision guard looks at disbursement.
- *SERVICING_HANDOFF* needs `servicingHandedOffAt`, which is not set.

items.title: Why a decision is refused while a check is pending
items.body:
`recordDecision` derives the current stage from the stored facts before it writes anything. With DOCUMENT_CHECK still PENDING, a required verification is not PASSED, so the derived stage is VERIFICATION, and the command throws `badRequest`, a **400** with the message about verification checks. No transaction is opened.

- *200, stage unchanged* is wrong: the guard throws before saving.
- *409* is wrong: the helper used is `badRequest`.
- *403* is wrong: underwriters hold `application:record-decision`; the refusal is about state, not role.

excerpts.quote: throw badRequest("All required verification checks must pass before decisioning.");

items.title: Start here: LedgerFlow Lending and its derived stage
items.body:
LedgerFlow Lending is a loan-origination workflow in Next.js, Prisma and PostgreSQL. An application moves through intake, verification, credit decisioning, conditions, approval, disbursement and the hand-off to servicing. No command ever sets the stage directly: after every write, a pure function recomputes it from the application's facts.

Read in this order:

1. `README.md`, including the security posture section (the login is a demo role switcher).
2. `docs/learning/guided-reading-path.md`: twelve stops through the code, each ending with a **Check**.
3. `docs/learning/concepts-demonstrated.md`: one concept per section, with where it falls short.
4. `docs/architecture/auth-and-permissions.md` and `request-lifecycle.md` when you want more detail.

Try each **Check** yourself before reading its answer line. The two files you will keep open are `src/services/workflow-reconciliation-service.ts` and `src/services/application-command-service.ts`.

excerpts.quote: The current stage is never set directly by a command.

readMore.why: Concepts, with where this code falls short.

items.title: Why an equal sequence number is applied again
items.body:
The apply test is `>=`, so an event whose sequence equals the stored one counts as fresh. The FAILED result overwrites PASSED. The out-of-order flag uses `<`, so the event is not marked out of order either. The concepts doc lists this among the guard's weaknesses: a provider that re-sends or reorders events with the same sequence can flip a result.

- *Ignored as already seen* would need `>` instead of `>=`.
- *Stored as out of order* would need the `<` test to be true, and 5 is not below 5.
- *Refused by a unique index* is wrong: events have no unique key on sequence.

items.title: Why a failed condition beats an approval
items.body:
With intake done and every required verification PASSED, the verification rule does not fire. The decisioning rule fires only for PENDING or REFER, so an APPROVED decision passes it. The next rule looks for any condition whose status is FAILED and returns CONDITIONS with a reason naming that condition. The APPROVED rule comes later and is never reached.

- *APPROVED* would need the APPROVED rule to come before the condition rules.
- *CREDIT_DECISIONING* is returned only for PENDING or REFER decisions.
- *VERIFICATION* is wrong: that rule looks at verifications, not conditions.

items.title: Why a reason-only change still writes a transition
items.body:
`reconcileAndPersistStage` writes when the derived stage differs from the stored one **or** the derived reason differs from `stageReason`. If only the reason changed, it still updates the row (bumping `stateVersion`) and creates an `ApplicationTransition` whose `fromStage` equals its `toStage`. The decision flow triggers this, because `recordDecision` overwrites `stageReason` with the underwriter's text and the reconciler then puts its own reason back.

- *Nothing* would need the stage comparison alone.
- *Reason only, no transition* is wrong: both writes are in the same branch.
- *Throws* is wrong: nothing forbids equal stages in a transition.

items.title: What happens to an out-of-order provider event
items.body:
The command compares the incoming `providerSequence` with the verification's stored one. 3 is below 5, so `isOutOfOrder` is true and `shouldApply` is false. The event row is still written, with `appliedToWorkflow: false` and `receivedOutOfOrder: true`, so history keeps it, but the verification itself is not updated and stays PASSED.

- *Becomes FAILED* is the bug the guard exists to stop.
- *Refused with 409* is wrong: nothing throws; the event is stored.
- *Dropped without a row* is wrong: `createExternalEvent` runs for every event.

excerpts.quote: const isOutOfOrder = input.providerSequence < verification.providerSequence; const shouldApply = input.providerSequence >= verification.providerSequence;

items.title: Why a servicing agent gets 404 on a pre-funding file
items.body:
Neither read route declares a permission, so the repository's visibility filter is the only gate. For SERVICING_AGENT it limits results to the DISBURSEMENT and SERVICING_HANDOFF stages. A file in CONDITIONS does not match, the lookup returns nothing, and the service throws `notFound`: **404** "Application not found."

- *200, no permission needed* is half right: no permission is declared, but the visibility filter still applies.
- *403* is wrong: the code reports a missing record, not a refused one.
- *200 with data hidden* is wrong: the record is not returned at all.
